notes:
I've written notes for every verse. Notes for vv. 1–16 are fairly full. Notes for vv. 17–29 are thinner because some pages cut off before reaching them, and I found nothing at all for vv. 22–23 and 26–27, so those verses are left out. Most of the debate is over v. 6 and, to a lesser degree, vv. 4, 7, 15 and 20.

**Missing material**
- I found no Lutheran, Pentecostal-specific or Catholic/Orthodox sources (newadvent, catholic.com, oca.org).
- I found nothing on bibleodyssey.org.
- I found no pages arguing for or against a prosperity-gospel reading.
- Precept Austin and the full Gill and Ellicott chapter pages didn't come up.
- Tradition labels such as "Methodist" for Adam Clarke and "Presbyterian" for Matthew Henry are my own general knowledge. The pages don't say so, so check them before printing.

---

**v. 1**
- Guzik says a good name is a kind of wealth worth more than riches. He quotes Trapp: riches last only until death, but a good name outlives you and is left behind as a blessing. He also quotes Bridges' warning that reputation can itself become vanity and a snare; the only safe honour comes from God. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-22/
- Pulpit Commentary: "good" in the Authorized Version is in italics, showing that the epithet is not expressed in the Hebrew, which is simply שֵׁם (shem), "name." It says the second line explains the first: a good name is so valuable because it wins affection and friendship, which are far preferable to material riches. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/proverbs-22.html
- Gill reads "favour" as above all favour with God, possibly "grace is better than silver and gold." Benson says that by great riches we may relieve men's bodily wants; but, by a good name, we may recommend religion to them. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/proverbs/22-1.htm
- NET note: "good favor" is a difficult phrase. It can mean favour gained, or engaging qualities that win the regard of others. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Pro&chapter=22

**v. 2**
- Guzik: rich and poor share one Creator, so neither should stereotype the other. He quotes Ross: God can as easily bring the rich low as raise the poor. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-22/
- NET note: the verb means rich and poor "meet together", living side by side. It rejects the reading that they *should* live together because they are God's creatures, saying the verb won't bear it. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Pro&chapter=22
- Matthew Henry: rich and poor meet at God's judgment seat and at his throne of grace. Each has a role: the rich to be charitable, the poor to grow in patience. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/proverbs/22.htm

**v. 3**
- Guzik: wisdom knows when to hide and let danger pass. The "simple" can't sense danger and suffer for it. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-22/
- NET note: "evil" here most likely means danger rather than sin. The verb for "suffer" originally meant "to be fined": the simple pay for blundering into trouble. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Pro&chapter=22
- Matthew Henry reads it spiritually: the prudent run to the Lord as a strong tower, as Noah and Joseph prepared ahead. Faith foresees the evil coming upon sinners, and looks to Jesus Christ as the sure refuge from the storm. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/proverbs/22-1.htm

**v. 4**
- Guzik: humility is the right view of self; the fear of the Lord is the right view of God. The humble can surely expect *spiritual* riches, honour and life, and often material ones in this world too. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-22/
- Matthew Henry limits the material promise: riches and long life "as far as God sees good." At the least it means spiritual riches and eternal life. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/proverbs/22.htm
- Trapp: the humble get "a sufficiency, if not a superfluity." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jtc/proverbs-22.html
- NET notes:
  - The word for "reward" is related to "heel", meaning what follows "on the heels of."
  - "Humility" here means piety.
  - Some scholars make "fear of the Lord" the first reward of humility, but the note thinks that less likely.
  https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Pro&chapter=22
- *Prosperity teaching:* I found no source on these sites discussing a prosperity reading of this verse.

**v. 5**
- Guzik quotes Waltke: the thorns are temptations such as easy sex and easy money. His application: if you want fewer temptations, change the road you're on. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-22/
- NET note: "thorns" is an unusual word, and some scholars amend it to "traps." NET keeps "thorns" as the harder reading. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Pro&chapter=22
- Matthew Henry: thorns of grief over past sins, and snares that pull a person into more sin. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/proverbs/22.htm

**v. 6 (the main point of disagreement)**
*Meaning of "train":*
- NET note: the verb means "train up; dedicate" and is used for dedicating houses and altars. It firmly rejects the popular sermon idea of rubbing date juice on a baby's palate, because that Arabic meaning appears almost a thousand years after Proverbs. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Pro&chapter=22
- Clarke reads it as dedicating the child to God first, then nursing and disciplining him as God's child. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-22/

*Meaning of "the way he should go" — two readings:*
- **According to the child's own nature and calling:**
  - Pulpit Commentary favours an injunction to consider the child's nature, faculties, and temperament. https://biblehub.com/proverbs/22-6.htm
  - Cambridge Bible stresses a careful study of individual character and capacity. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/proverbs/22-6.htm
  - Guzik, quoting Kidner and Morgan, holds both senses: the child's individual bent and the path of wisdom. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-22/
  - Trevin Wax (TGC) says it means showing how a child might utilize their own gifts and abilities in the fulfillment of their God-given vocation. https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/blogs/trevin-wax/train-up-a-parent/
- **The one right way:**
  - NET note: Proverbs knows only two ways, wise and foolish. It says the verse does not support the modern psychological reading "train a child according to his personality trait." https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Pro&chapter=22
  - Matthew Henry: train them not in the way they would go, that of their corrupt hearts, but in the way they should go. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/proverbs/22-6.htm
- **An ironic reading** (raised, not adopted, by Desiring God): the verse could be a warning, as in Clifford: let a boy do what he wants and he'll become a self-willed adult. The article rejects it. https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/train-up-a-child-in-the-way-he-should-go

*Promise or principle?*
- **Principle, not guarantee:**
  - Desiring God (Baptist site): not a hard-and-fast promise to parents, however, for the rest of the book makes clear that the power of the youth's future depends not only on the parents' guidance. https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/train-up-a-child-in-the-way-he-should-go
  - Trevin Wax (TGC): To interpret Proverbs 22:6 as a promise without exceptions is to misread the genre. https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/blogs/trevin-wax/train-up-a-parent/
  - NET note: proverbs are not universal truths. One can anticipate positive results from careful child-training – but there may be an occasional exception. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Pro&chapter=22
  - Matthew Henry (Presbyterian): many trained children depart, Solomon included, but early training may help them come back. At the least, the parents have done their duty. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/proverbs/22.htm
- **A middle view (Enduring Word, the site in your Pentecostal/charismatic group):** Guzik calls it a principle, proven by Solomon's own life, that the Holy Spirit may "quicken" into a promise for troubled parents. He quotes Waltke that the book is addressed to youths, not parents. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-22/
- **Closer to a promise:**
  - Adam Clarke (Methodist): if these things are done, the child (you have God's word for it) will never depart from the path of life. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/amp/proverbs/22-6.html
  - An older bible.org article: This is a promise, not merely a warning. https://bible.org/seriespage/6-principle-nurture-training-your-child

*Text note:*
- Cambridge Bible: All the early manuscripts of the Septuagint omit this verse. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/proverbs/22-6.htm
- Douay-Rheims begins the verse "It is a proverb." https://biblehub.com/proverbs/22-6.htm

**v. 7**
- Guzik quotes Garrett: borrow only as a last resort and get out of debt quickly. Guzik himself says the wise aim to be lenders, not borrowers. He quotes Ross that the verse may refer to Israelites selling themselves into slavery for debt. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-22/
- NET note: an observation on life showing how poverty makes people dependent on others. "Slave" may refer to debt-slavery under Exodus 21. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Pro&chapter=22
- Matthew Henry: the rich often rule "with pride and rigour"; keep out of debt as far as possible. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/proverbs/22.htm
- Bible Hub's study page calls it a matter-of-fact observation, not an endorsement. https://biblehub.com/proverbs/22-7.htm
- Bible Hub's Q&A page is much stricter: The verse is not hyperbole; it is a literal warning that financial obligation creates real bondage. https://biblehub.com/q/Lesson_on_debt_and_financial_duty.htm
- Pulpit: the Septuagint reads differently, "household servants will lend to their own masters" - a reading on which some of the Fathers have commented. https://biblehub.com/proverbs/22-7.htm

**v. 8**
- Guzik: sins are seeds that bring a harvest. "The rod of his anger will fail" means the sinner has no defence when the harvest comes. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-22/
- NET note: the oppressor will no longer be able to unleash his fury on others. The Septuagint adds a line, "God blesses a cheerful giver" (compare 2 Cor 9:7). https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Pro&chapter=22
- Matthew Henry: ill-gotten gain doesn't prosper, and abused power doesn't last. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/proverbs/22.htm

**v. 9**
- NET notes: "generous" is literally "good of eye", the opposite of the covetous "evil eye." "Blessed" here means enriched. By blessing the giver, God is in fact providing for the poor. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Pro&chapter=22
- Guzik: God won't let anyone out-give him. He quotes Trapp that "his bread" may mean food spared from the giver's own meal. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-22/
- Matthew Henry: the giver shares "of" his bread, not all of it. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/proverbs/22.htm

**v. 10**
- Guzik: strife comes from *people*; remove the scoffer and the quarrelling stops. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-22/
- NET note: the scorner is the one Proverbs says can't be changed by correction. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Pro&chapter=22
- Matthew Henry gives the example of Ishmael being sent away for mocking Isaac. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/proverbs/22.htm

**v. 11**
- Guzik: inner purity shows in gracious words, and this wins friends in high places, and fellowship with God. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-22/
- Matthew Henry describes the honest, well-spoken counsellor. He notes that some read "the king" as the King of kings, or the Messiah. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/proverbs/22.htm

**v. 12**
- Guzik quotes Garrett: God exposes the distortions of the faithless. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-22/
- Matthew Henry: God's providence keeps the knowledge of himself alive in the world despite Satan's efforts. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/proverbs/22.htm

**v. 13**
- Guzik quotes Spurgeon (those with little to do have the most to say) and Waltke on the lazy man's absurd excuses. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-22/
- Matthew Henry: the sluggard fears an imaginary lion but ignores the real one, the devil, "which is in bed with him." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/proverbs/22.htm

**v. 14**
- Matthew Henry: a warning to young men against sexual sin. Falling into this pit shows a person already left to himself by God as judgment for other sins, and few climb out. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/proverbs/22.htm

**v. 15**
- Gill: the folly is inborn sin. The rod is a means of making children wise, and of restraining the folly that is bound up in them. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/n84/proverbs/22-15.html
- Matthew Henry: corruption is woven into our nature, and gentle methods alone won't remove it. He applies the verse to God's discipline of us too (Heb 12). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/proverbs/22.htm
- Bible Hub study notes: the rod means firm correction given with self-control, not uncontrolled anger or cruelty. Also: No parental correction can regenerate the heart. https://biblehub.com/proverbs/22-15.htm
- *Is the rod literal?*
  - GotQuestions: taken literally these proverbs mean corporal punishment, but they have application beyond physical discipline. The primary point of the biblical proverb is that loving discipline benefits the child. https://www.gotquestions.org/spare-rod-spoil-child.html
  - TGC (Tilly Dillehay) defends spanking as a way to show children what God's loving discipline is like. https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/article/rod-point-children-god/
  - I found no source on these sites arguing against corporal punishment.

**v. 16**
- Matthew Henry: such people refuse to help the poor, or exploit them, while flattering the rich with gifts or bribes. "Many have been beggared by a foolish generosity, but never any by a prudent charity." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/proverbs/22.htm
- Guzik (Spanish edition): giving to the rich is like oppressing the poor, because both lack compassion for the needy. https://es.enduringword.com/comentario-biblico/proverbios-22/

**vv. 17–21 (introduction to the "thirty sayings")**
- Guzik: a new section runs from 22:17 to 24:22, with longer sayings grouped by theme. "Keep them within you" is literally "in thy belly", meaning held in the heart and memory. https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/guzik_david/study-guide/proverbs/proverbs-22.cfm
- Matthew Henry: from here to the end of ch. 24 Solomon speaks directly to "thee", "even to thee." Preachers should likewise preach *to* hearers, not just in front of them. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/proverbs/22.htm
- TGC commentary: the goal is to make the student a reliable source of wisdom for the royal court, "those who sent you" (see v. 29). https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/commentary/proverbs/
- *v. 20 and the Egyptian connection:*
  - NET note: older versions read "excellent things," "officers" or "heretofore," but the word should be rendered "thirty," referring to the number in the collection. https://classic.net.bible.org/passage.php?passage=Pro+22%3A17--24%3A34%3B30%3A1-33%3B31%3A1-9
  - NET also notes the section's great similarity to the Instruction of Amenemope in Egypt. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Pro&chapter=22
  - Guzik, following Waltke, says Solomon borrowed Amenemope's structure but not its content. https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/guzik_david/study-guide/proverbs/proverbs-22.cfm
  - TGC course: The most significant difference between the two is the devotion to the Lord exhibited in Proverbs. https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/course/knowing-the-bible-proverbs/
  - GotQuestions: scholars have debated the exact relationship for about a hundred years, over which text influenced the other. https://www.gotquestions.org/Instruction-of-Amenemope.html

**vv. 24–25**
- NET note: avoid a hothead because his influence could be fatal (a similar idea is found in the Instruction of Amenemope, chap. 9). https://classic.net.bible.org/passage.php?passage=Pro+22%3A17--24%3A34%3B30%3A1-33%3B31%3A1-9

**v. 28**
- NET note: this saying is about respecting other people's property, and parallels Amenemope chapter 6. https://classic.net.bible.org/passage.php?passage=Pro+22%3A17--24%3A34%3B30%3A1-33%3B31%3A1-9

**v. 29**
- NET note: true skill earns recognition and advancement, comparing Amenemope chapter 30. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Pro&chapter=22
- TGC links this verse back to "those who sent you" in v. 21. https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/commentary/proverbs/
